question:
Patient note:
A 43-year-old woman is interviewed this afternoon in the pre-induction bay before the general surgery team brings her to the theatre for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy that is expected to take ninety minutes under general anaesthesia with a single overnight stay on the short-stay surgical ward. Three weeks earlier she was admitted through the emergency department with fever to 39.4 °C, rigors, right-upper-quadrant pain, hypotension in the low 80s mm Hg systolic, and a serum lactate of 3.8 mmol/L; blood cultures eventually grew Escherichia coli and an abdominal ultrasound demonstrated gallbladder wall thickening with pericholecystic fluid. Broad-spectrum antibiotics and percutaneous cholecystostomy rapidly reversed the septic picture, and she was discharged ten days ago on culture-directed oral levofloxacin. Because peripheral veins had become sclerosed after several days of pressor infusions, a right basilic peripherally inserted central catheter was placed on hospital day two and remains in situ for completion of the antimicrobial course; the dressing is clean and dry today, with brisk blood return and no tenderness or erythema along the catheter tract. She has not returned to an operating room, endoscopy suite, or interventional radiology bay since the index drainage procedure and reports no other hospitalisations, invasive interventions, or major operations in the past several years, including none within the last 30 days. Over the last week she resumed her usual routine of cycling five miles to work, climbing a flight of stairs to her office, and walking her dog each evening, so her baseline ambulation is intact without limitation. She denies orthopnoea, exertional dyspnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling, or episodes of chest discomfort; a transthoracic echocardiogram ordered during the septic admission to evaluate tachycardia showed normal biventricular size with an ejection fraction of 60 % and no valvular pathology. Review of systems is negative for cough, sputum production, recent colds, pleuritic pain, or any episode of pneumonia in the past month. She has never required a plaster cast, crutches, wheelchair, or prolonged bed rest, and she has avoided fractures or high-energy trauma. She also confirms that she has not worn any immobilising splints or braces over the past month. Neurologically she reports no focal deficits, transient ischaemic events, or limb paresis. The patient volunteers that cosmetic concerns led her to seek evaluation for serpiginous blue veins along the medial calves that first appeared during her second pregnancy; duplex imaging done by a vascular clinic last year confirmed superficial reflux without deep-vein involvement, and she wears 15–20 mm Hg knee-high compression stockings at work for comfort. She emphasizes that her legs have never become painful, warm, or asymmetrically swollen and that no clinician has suggested sonography for suspected clot. A detailed personal and family history reveals no prior episodes of deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolus, miscarriages, or clotting disorders among first-degree relatives. After her cholecystostomy she underwent a thrombophilia screen because routine chemistry panels showed a mild but persistent elevation of total homocysteine to 18 µmol/L; vitamin B₁₂ and folate levels were normal, and genetic assays were negative for Factor V Leiden mutation or prothrombin G20210A variant. She has never used oestrogen-containing contraception, selective oestrogen receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or chronic corticosteroids. She has no history of Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, or other inflammatory bowel disorders and has never been diagnosed with chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Current medications include oral levofloxacin 500 mg once daily, cholecalciferol 1000 IU, and an over-the-counter ibuprofen tablet taken occasionally for menstrual cramping; she stopped all non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs 72 hours ago per anaesthesia instructions. She neither smokes nor uses recreational drugs and drinks wine only on holidays. Vital signs obtained fifteen minutes ago show temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg, pulse 82 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air; body mass index is 24 kg/m². She appears calm, conversant, and in no acute distress while lying supine on the stretcher. Jugular venous pulse is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk, and heart sounds are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen displays a soft, non-distended contour with mild tenderness beneath the right costal margin and no rebound or guarding; the cholecystostomy site in the mid-axillary line has closed around a 1-cm scar without drainage. Lower extremity examination reveals several dilated tortuous superficial veins over the posteromedial calf bilaterally that become more prominent when the legs dangle, but calf circumferences are equal, the skin is warm, and gentle dorsiflexion elicits no discomfort or cord. Neurologic screening discloses intact cranial nerves, full strength, and symmetric reflexes. Laboratory data drawn through the PICC this morning demonstrate haemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, haematocrit 40 %, platelets 255 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 7.1 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, creatinine 0.86 mg/dL, AST 30 U/L, ALT 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.0 s with an international normalised ratio of 1.0, activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s, and a repeat homocysteine of 17 µmol/L. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram reads normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats per minute with no ST-T abnormalities. A portable chest radiograph shows clear lung fields and catheter tip projecting over the cavo-atrial junction. An ultrasound of the hepatobiliary tree obtained yesterday demonstrates decompression of the gallbladder and no common-bile-duct dilation. She has been fasting since midnight, sequential compression sleeves are at the bedside but have not yet been applied, and pre-operative antibiotic prophylaxis will be administered in the operating room once final checks are complete.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini perioperative VTE risk score sums the weights of qualifying risk factors at the preoperative assessment:
- Age 41–60 years: she is 43 → 1.
- Varicose veins: tortuous superficial calf veins with documented reflux → 1.
- Sepsis within the past month: E. coli sepsis three weeks ago → 1.
- Laparoscopic surgery lasting >45 minutes: planned cholecystectomy is expected to take 90 minutes → 2. Count this operation once.
- Central venous access: the PICC remains in place with its tip at the cavoatrial junction → 2.
- Elevated serum homocysteine: repeat level 17 µmol/L confirms the elevation → 3.
No additional points are supported: BMI is 24 kg/m², she is fully ambulatory, and no separate recent major operation, prior VTE, or family history of VTE is reported.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10.
Final answer: 10
